# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. The series argues for universal background checks (UBC) and an assault weapons ban (AWB); copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and year. Population and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Headline toll: total gun deaths (CDC). Breakdowns by intent go in the appendix.
B3. Children and teens: "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; give the age range in the appendix.
B4. Background checks: use the Miller, Hepburn & Azrael (2017) estimate (22%).
B5. Mass shootings: GVA counts; GVA's definition in the appendix.
B6. Rifle share of homicides: if it comes up, one sentence, then mass-casualty lethality.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

 Gun Violence Widely Viewed as a Major – and Growing – National Problem 

 1. Views of U.S. gun laws, impact of gun ownership on safety 

 2. Americans’ views of specific gun policy proposals 

 Acknowledgments 

 Methodology 

 Several policy proposals that would further restrict access to guns or ammunition continue to receive support from majorities of Americans. Smaller shares of Americans support several more permissive policy proposals.

 Roughly nine-in-ten U.S. adults (88%) favor preventing people with mental illness from purchasing guns, while 79% favor increasing the minimum age for buying guns to 21 years old.

 Sizable majorities also support banning high-capacity ammunition magazines that hold more than 10 rounds (66%) and banning assault-style weapons (64%).

 Four policy proposals that would ease restrictions on guns, including allowing people to carry concealed guns without a permit, draw less support from the public.

 Half of Americans favor allowing teachers and school officials to carry guns in K-12 schools, while 44% say people should be able to carry concealed guns in more places. Fewer than a third of Americans favor shortening waiting periods for gun purchases (30%) or allowing concealed carry without a permit (24%).

 Views by party

 Overwhelming majorities of both Democrats (89%) and Republicans (88%) favor preventing people with mental illnesses from purchasing guns. Majorities in both parties support increasing the minimum age for buying guns to 21 years old, though support for this policy is more widespread among Democrats (90%) than Republicans (69%).

 There are wider partisan differences on the other policy proposals in the survey. While large majorities of Democrats favor banning high-capacity ammunition magazines (85%) and banning assault-style weapons (85%), fewer than half of Republicans support either of these two proposals (45% and 42%, respectively).

 By contrast, while seven-in-ten or more Republicans favor allowing teachers and school officials to carry guns in K-12 schools (74%) or allowing people to carry concealed guns in more places (71%), fewer than three-in-ten Democrats support these policies. Republicans are also more likely than Democrats to favor shortening waiting periods for people who want to buy guns legally (45% vs. 16%) and allowing people to carry concealed guns without a permit (40% vs. 9%), though both of these proposals have more opposition than support among those in both parties.

 Views of gun policies among gun owners, non-owners

 While nearly nine-in-ten gun owners (87%) and non-owners (89%) both favor preventing people with mental illnesses from purchasing guns, there are wider gaps between gun owners and non-owners on other policy proposals.

 Non-owners are at least 30 percentage points more likely than gun owners to favor banning high-capacity ammunition magazines (78% vs. 45%) or banning assault-style weapons (77% vs. 43%). They are also 18 points more likely to favor increasing the minimum age for buying guns to 21 years old, though majorities in both groups favor this (86% vs. 68%).

 Gun owners are 37 points more likely than non-owners to favor allowing people to carry concealed guns in more places (68% vs. 31%), and 30 points more likely to favor allowing teachers and school officials to carry guns in K-12 schools (69% vs. 39%).

 Few non-owners favor shortened waiting periods (22%) or allowing concealed carry without a permit (14%). Gun owners are more supportive of these policies, with 44% favoring shorter waiting periods for people who want to buy guns legally and 41% supporting allowing people to carry concealed guns without a permit. Still, majorities of gun owners oppose these policy proposals.

 Gun owners’, non-owners’ views by political party

 Across seven of the eight policy proposals asked about in the survey, gun owners within each political party are more likely than non-owners of the same party to favor policies that expand access to guns and ammunition.

 Non-owners are more likely to favor policies that are more restrictive – though differences are generally larger among Republicans and Republican leaners than among Democrats and Democratic leaners.

 At the same time, the wide partisan differences on these questions are seen among both gun owners and non-owners (Two-in-ten Democrats and 45% of Republicans say they personally own a gun).

 For example, nearly nine-in-ten Democrats who do not own a gun favor banning high-capacity magazines (89%), a view held by a smaller – though still wide – majority of Democrats who report owning a gun (73%). Meanwhile, a narrower majority of Republicans who do not own a gun (60%) favor this policy, compared with roughly half as many Republican gun owners (31%).

 A large majority of Republicans who own guns (85%) favor allowing teachers to carry guns in K-12 schools, as do 64% of Republicans who do not own a gun. Among Democrats, 34% of gun owners favor this, as do 25% of non-owners.

Survey finds bipartisan support for gun violence prevention policies | Association of Health Care Journalists 

 Survey finds bipartisan support for gun violence prevention policies | Association of Health Care Journalists 

 Firearm Violence 

 •

 Analysis 

 Survey finds broad, bipartisan support for gun violence prevention policies

 Kaitlin Washburn 

 September 15, 2025 

 Share:

 Photo by David Maiolo (CC BY-SA 3.0)

 Both gun owners and non-gun owners across political lines widely support gun violence prevention policies, a new survey from the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions found. 

 The survey, conducted in January, included nearly 3,000 respondents, a third of whom were gun owners. Of the respondents, 959 were Republicans and 1,419 were Democrats.

 Respondents signaled support for a broad array of gun violence prevention policies, including safe storage laws, ownership licensing from local law enforcement, extreme risk protection orders and government funding for violence prevention efforts like social services and conflict mediation. 

 This survey, and others like it, can inform reporting on gun violence prevention because they gauge the public’s understanding and opinion of key policies. Knowing the attitudes of both gun owners and non-gun owners also helps provide an accurate picture of what those two groups think. 

 Surveys are also good jumping off points for stories because they emphasize the value of interviewing gun owners. Seek out gun owners in your area to find out how they feel about these policies and their overall thoughts on gun violence prevention. Or, if your city or state is considering enacting any of these policies, this survey might help inform the public’s perspective on the policy. 

 Findings 

 The survey asked participants about their support for several different gun policies. 

 About 74% of all respondents support laws requiring a person to lock their guns up at home when they’re not in use. Roughly 62% of gun owners support that policy, while 81% of non-gun owners do. 

 Nearly three-quarters of participants (72%) said people should be required to obtain a license from law enforcement before buying a firearm. Just over half of gun owners (61%) agreed with that policy. 

 Source: National Survey of Gun Policy | Center for Gun Violence Solutions (publichealth.jhu.edu) 

 There was also broad support for funding and supporting community violence intervention programs that provide social services, outreach and conflict mediation. Overall, 72% of respondents support those programs, and of that, 67% of gun owners and 74% of non-gun owners said they’re supportive. 

 Over three-quarters of respondents support allowing family members, law enforcement and/or health care clinicians to temporarily remove a gun from a loved one at risk of harming themselves or others. 

 Notably, about 70% of gun owners support extreme risk protection orders. 

 The vast majority of people surveyed (82%) said they support prohibiting a person subject to a temporary domestic violence protection order from having a gun for the duration of the order.

 Less than a quarter of respondents said they support people carrying loaded guns in public without a permit or license. Over one-third of Republicans (36%) and gun owners (37%) support permitless carry. 

 Recent coverage  

 The Trace recently reported on another study examining gun owners’ thoughts on gun regulation. 

 The study, commissioned in 2019 not long after the Parkland school shooting, sought to “determine the most effective ways of communicating with the American public about the benefits of firearm ownership,” according to The Trace. 

 The study, titled “Communicating With The American Public About Firearm Ownership,” found that Americans supportive of gun ownership could be persuaded to support policies regulating guns, such as background checks, red flag laws and a gun registry. 

 The study, commissioned by the National Shooting Sports Foundation, involved an online survey that tested the power of 24 pro-gun and 24 anti-gun messages. Over 4,000 Americans responded. 

 “While the sports shooting industry devotes substantial funding and effort to communications initiatives to boost participation in and support for sport shooting and firearms,” the study notes, according to The Trace, “little reliable data exists indicating which messages and communications themes work best.” 

 The findings were never made public, according to The Trace. Yet these findings offer key insights into how gun owners feel about crucial gun laws.

{"path": "/workspace/out/brief.md", "content": "# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026**

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Guns killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, an average of one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year (CDC, 2023).
- The federal background-check requirement stops at the dealer's door. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases involved no check at all (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- Mass shootings rose again in 2023, to 656 incidents that killed 712 people (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). Peer-reviewed research finds mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban (DiMaggio et al., 2019). Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023 (CDC, 2023). That averages out to one death every 11 minutes: 128 people a day, every day, for the entire year. Each of those deaths left an empty chair somewhere, at a kitchen table, in a classroom, on a shift that never ended.

A toll like that is not weather, and it is not geography. It is the accumulation of choices made by the one institution with the power to change them. For more than 30 years Congress has declined to close the two gaps that most define American gun violence: a background-check law that reaches only part of the gun market, and the absence, since 2004, of any federal limit on assault weapons. Year after year, the cost of that refusal is counted in cemeteries, hospital wards and classrooms that will never be full again.

This brief is about both gaps, and about what the evidence says Congress should do about them. The numbers that follow are not abstractions. They are the price of the loopholes, and every one of them is a policy choice the current Congress can reverse.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate should land harder than this one: guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, and they have been for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In 2023 alone, guns killed 2,566 children and teens, an average of seven young people every day (CDC, 2023). Firearms now kill more children and teens than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, 2025).

Every one of those deaths was preventable in the specific ways this brief describes: a sale that could have gone through a background check, a military-style rifle that could have been off the civilian market, a person in crisis whose firearms a court could have temporarily removed. A country that knows the leading cause of death for its children and still declines to act on it is not out of ideas. It is out of will.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, federal law has required a background check on gun purchases from licensed dealers. The requirement ends at the shop counter. Federal law requires no check on most private sales, including many arranged online or at gun shows, which means a person legally barred from having a gun can buy one from an unlicensed seller without ever being screened.

The data show how much of the market slips through. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among private purchases, including person-to-person sales arranged in person, online or at gun shows, half were obtained without a check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Universal background checks close the gap by routing every sale and transfer through the same federal screening system licensed dealers already use. Nothing about it is experimental: the check takes minutes, it is endorsed across medicine, public health and law enforcement, and 86 percent of American adults support requiring background checks on all gun sales and transfers (McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023).

Closing the private-sale gap is the most basic step available to Congress, and it has been sitting on the table for more than 30 years. A loophole that lets half of private gun purchases proceed with no background check is not a detail of the law. It is the law failing at the moment it matters most.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings rose again in 2023. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, roughly one every 13 hours, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692 (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). That is up from 647 in 2022 and second only to the record 689 of 2021.

The weapons involved are no mystery. In Uvalde, Texas, in 2022, a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School with an AR-15-style rifle (ABC News, 2022). In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, a gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds at a bowling alley before attacking a second location, killing 18 people in all (Maine Independent Commission, 2024). From Parkland in 2018 onward, the country's deadliest attacks keep featuring the same signature: semiautomatic rifles built for rapid fire at close range, fed by detachable high-capacity magazines.

Congress has already tested the alternative. The federal assault weapons ban was in force from 1994 until Congress allowed it to lapse in 2004. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting data from 1981 through 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely to occur in years the ban was in force, a statistically significant difference after controlling for the underlying trend, equal to nine fewer mass-shooting deaths for every 10,000 firearm homicides (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). The same study found that assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 mass-shooting fatalities documented in its dataset, about 86 percent.

Banning assault weapons is majority opinion, not radical politics. Sixty-four percent of Americans favor a ban, and 66 percent favor prohibiting the high-capacity magazines that make these rifles so lethal in close quarters (Pew Research Center, June 2023).

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that federal law has left open for more than three decades. The policy is backed by 86 percent of American adults (McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023).

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban that lapsed in 2004 and update its definitions to cover the rifles and detachable high-capacity magazines on the market today. A 64 percent majority of Americans supports a ban (Pew Research Center, June 2023), and the evidence indicates it worked: mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely in the ban years (DiMaggio et al., 2019).

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Sustain and expand the dedicated federal research funding Congress began in fiscal 2020, when it provided $25 million for the CDC and NIH after more than two decades without any (U.S. Senate Committee on Appropriations, December 2019). The country cannot prevent what it declines to measure.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Offer grants to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others. Seventy-seven percent of Americans support these laws, including about 70 percent of gun owners (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, January 2025), and Connecticut's version is estimated to have averted roughly one suicide for every 10 gun removals (Swanson et al., 2017).

## Closing the gaps

The gaps in federal gun law were not discovered in nature. Congress wrote the private-sale gap into the Brady Act in 1993 and allowed the assault weapons ban to lapse in 2004. What Congress wrote, Congress can close. The evidence is in, the public is behind it, and the deaths continue at a rate of one every 11 minutes. The only question left is how many more empty chairs the country will count while Congress decides.

---

**About the author.** Dr. Jamal Whitfield is Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at the Northgate Progress Institute, where he leads the Safer Communities series.

*All statistics in this brief are sourced and documented in the accompanying data appendix (Safer Communities Brief No. 9, Data Appendix).*

*Production draft for editorial review under NPI-PUB-2026-0457. Not for release until approved by the Director of Publications.*

---
# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026**

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Guns killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, an average of one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth year in a row (CDC, 2023).
- Federal background checks stop at the dealer's door: 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases involved no check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- Mass shootings rose again in 2023, to 656 incidents that killed 712 people (Gun Violence Archive, 2024). Peer-reviewed research finds mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## The toll

In 2023, 46,728 people died from gun violence in the United States (CDC, 2023). That is one death every 11 minutes, around the clock, all year: 128 people a day who did not come home. [128/day = derived: note in appendix.] Each of those deaths left an empty chair, at a kitchen table, in a classroom, at a worksite. ...

The toll is not weather. It is policy. The United States is alone among wealthy nations in treating this scale of death as the cost of doing nothing, and Congress has spent three decades confirming that judgment. Two failures of federal law drive it: a background-check requirement that covers only some sales, and the absence of any federal limit on assault weapons since the last ban expired.

Hmm, "alone among wealthy nations in treating this scale of death as the cost of doing nothing" — rhetorical claim, no specific stat. OK.

## Children and teens

No number in this debate lands harder than this one: guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, and they have been for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). Guns now kill more young people than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, 2025). In 2023 alone, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire, an average of seven every day (CDC, 2023).

[Wait: "for four consecutive years" — the source says "for the past four years" — i.e., 2020-2023. "for the fourth year in a row" (UPI: "For the fourth year in a row"). OK.]

Every one of those deaths was preventable in the specific ways this brief describes: a sale that could have required a check, a weapon designed for the battlefield that could have been off the civilian market, a person in crisis whose firearms could have been temporarily removed. [This previews recs.]

## The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, federal law has required a background check for gun purchases from licensed dealers. The requirement ends at the shop counter. Most private sales in the United States, including many arranged online or at gun shows, require no check under federal law, which means a person legally barred from owning a gun can buy one anyway.

The data show exactly how big that gap is. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases, including online and gun show sales, involved no check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Universal background checks close the gap: every sale and transfer would run through the same federal check system that dealers already use. This is not a fringe idea. It is endorsed across medicine, public health and law enforcement, and 81 percent of Americans support background checks for all gun purchasers (Monmouth University Poll, April 2023). It is also the least Congress can do: a check that takes minutes, for a toll that takes 46,728 lives a year.

## Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings rose again in 2023. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, roughly one every 13 hours, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 were injured (Gun Violence Archive, 2024). That is up from 647 in 2022 and second only to the record 689 in 2021.

The weapons in the deadliest attacks are no mystery. In Uvalde, Texas, in 2022, a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School with an AR-15-style rifle (ABC News, 2022). From Parkland in 2018 to Lewiston in 2023, the deadliest attacks of the past decade keep featuring the same class of weapon: semiautomatic rifles built for rapid fire at close range, fed by detachable magazines.

Congress has already run the experiment. The federal assault weapons ban was in force from 1994 until Congress let it lapse in 2004. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting data from 1981 through 2017 found mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely to occur in years the ban was in force, a statistically significant reduction after controlling for the underlying trend (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). The same study found assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 mass-shooting fatalities documented in its dataset, about 86 percent.

Banning assault weapons is majority opinion, not radical politics. Sixty-four percent of Americans favor a ban, and 66 percent favor banning the high-capacity magazines that make these rifles so lethal (Pew Research Center, June 2023).

## Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that federal law has left open for more than three decades. Eighty-one percent of Americans support it (Monmouth University Poll, April 2023).

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban that lapsed in 2004, extend its definitions to the rifles and magazines on the market today, and pair it with limits on high-capacity magazines (Pew Research Center, June 2023). The evidence says it saves lives: mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely in the ban years (DiMaggio et al., 2019).

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Sustain and expand the $25 million annual investment Congress first provided in fiscal 2020, after more than two decades with no dedicated federal research funding (U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee, 2019). You cannot prevent what you refuse to measure.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Offer grants to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people in crisis. Seventy-seven percent of Americans support these laws, including about 70 percent of gun owners (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, January 2025), and Connecticut's version is estimated to have averted roughly one suicide for every 10 gun removals (Swanson et al., 2017).

## Closing the gaps

The gaps in federal gun law were not discovered; they were written, by Congress, in 1993 and 1994, and preserved by Congress ever since. [Hmm, careful: the gaps were written by leaving private sales out of the Brady Act (1993) and letting the AWB lapse (2004). Phrase: "written into the Brady Act in 1993 and left open when the ban lapsed in 2004."] What Congress wrote, Congress can close. It has the evidence. It has the public. Every day it waits costs another 128 lives.

About the author: Dr. Jamal Whitfield is Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at the Northgate Progress Institute.

*All figures in this brief are sourced and documented in the accompanying data appendix.*

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026**

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

---

## Executive summary

- Guns killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, an average of one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year (CDC, 2023).
- The federal background-check requirement stops at the dealer's door. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases involved no check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- Mass shootings rose again in 2023, to 656 incidents that killed 712 people (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). Peer-reviewed research finds mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban (DiMaggio et al., 2019). Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023 (CDC, 2023). That averages one death every 11 minutes and 128 deaths every day, around the clock, for the entire year. Each one left an empty chair at a kitchen table, in a classroom, at a worksite.

Numbers like these do not happen to a country. They are chosen, one appropriations bill and one filibuster at a time, by the only government that can change them. The United States has run this experiment for three decades, and the result is a level of gun deaths that no peer nation would tolerate for a week. [Hmm — "no peer nation would tolerate" — rhetorical, fine.]

Two failures of federal law do most of the damage this brief is about: a background-check system that covers only part of the gun market, and the complete absence, since 2004, of any federal limit on assault weapons. Both were written by Congress. Both can be unwritten by Congress.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate should land harder than this one: guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, and they have been for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In 2023 alone, guns killed 2,566 children and teens, an average of seven young people every day (CDC, 2023). Firearms now kill more children and teens than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, 2025).

Every one of those 2,566 deaths was preventable in the specific, practical ways this brief describes: a sale that could have required a background check, a military-style rifle that could have been off the civilian market, a person in crisis whose firearms could have been temporarily removed by a court. A country that knows the leading cause of death for its children and declines to act on it is not out of ideas. It is out of will.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, federal law has required a background check on gun purchases from licensed dealers. The requirement ends at the shop counter. Federal law does not require a check on most private sales, including many arranged online or at gun shows, which means a person legally barred from having a gun can buy one from an unlicensed seller without ever being screened.

The data show how much of the market slips through. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among private purchases, including person-to-person sales arranged online or at gun shows, half were obtained without a check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Universal background checks close the gap by routing every sale and transfer through the same federal screening system dealers already use. The policy is endorsed across medicine, public health and law enforcement, and it commands overwhelming public support: 81 percent of Americans, including majorities in both parties, back background checks for all gun purchasers (Monmouth University Poll, April 2023). Actually Monmouth's release likely says "large majorities of Republicans and Democrats," but I can't confirm. Drop it.]

Closing the private-sale gap is the single most basic step available to Congress, and it has been sitting on the table for more than 30 years.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings rose again in 2023. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, roughly one every 13 hours, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692 (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). That is up from 647 in 2022 and second only to the record 689 of 2021.

The weapons involved are no mystery. In Uvalde, Texas, in 2022, a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School with an AR-15-style rifle (ABC News, 2022). In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, a gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds at a bowling alley before attacking a second location, killing 18 people in all (Maine Independent Commission, 2024). From Parkland in 2018 onward, the country's deadliest attacks keep featuring the same signature: semiautomatic rifles built for rapid fire at close range and fed by detachable magazines.

Congress has already tested the alternative. The federal assault weapons ban was in force from 1994 until Congress let it lapse in 2004. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting data from 1981 through 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely to occur in years the ban was in force, a statistically significant difference after controlling for the underlying trend, amounting to nine fewer mass-shooting deaths for every 10,000 firearm homicides (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). The same study found that assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 mass-shooting fatalities documented in its dataset, about 86 percent.

Banning assault weapons is majority opinion, not radical politics. Sixty-four percent of Americans favor a ban, and 66 percent favor prohibiting the high-capacity magazines that make these rifles so lethal in close quarters (Pew Research Center, June 2023).

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that federal law has left open for more than three decades. The policy is backed by 81 percent of Americans (Monmouth University Poll, April 2023).

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban that lapsed in 2004 and update its definitions to cover the rifles and detachable magazines on the market today. A 64 percent majority of Americans supports a ban (Pew Research Center, June 2023), and the evidence indicates it worked: mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely in the ban years (DiMaggio et al., 2019).

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Sustain and expand the $25 million annual research investment Congress first provided in fiscal 2020, after more than two decades without dedicated federal research funding (U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee, December 2019). The country cannot prevent what it declines to measure.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Offer grants to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection orders, which let courts temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be dangerous to themselves or others. Seventy-seven percent of Americans support these laws, including roughly 70 percent of gun owners (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, January 2025), and Connecticut's version is estimated to have averted about one suicide for every 10 gun removals (Swanson et al., 2017).

## Closing the gaps

The gaps in federal gun law were not discovered in nature. Congress wrote the private-sale gap into the Brady Act in 1993 and voted to let the assault weapons ban die in 2004. Every year of delay costs another 46,728 chances to have done the right thing.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026**

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

---

## Executive summary

- Guns killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, an average of one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year (CDC, 2023).
- The federal background-check requirement stops at the dealer's door. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases involved no check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- Mass shootings rose again in 2023, to 656 incidents that killed 712 people (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). Peer-reviewed research finds mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban (DiMaggio et al., 2019). Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023 (CDC, 2023). That averages one death every 11 minutes and 128 deaths every day, around the clock, for the entire year. Each one left an empty chair at a kitchen table, in a classroom, at a worksite.

Numbers like these do not happen to a country. They are chosen, one appropriations bill and one filibuster at a time, by the only government that can change them. The United States has run this experiment for three decades, and the result is a level of gun deaths that no peer nation would tolerate for a week. [Hmm — "no peer nation would tolerate" — rhetorical, fine.]

Two failures of federal law do most of the damage this brief is about: a background-check system that covers only part of the gun market, and the complete absence, since 2004, of any federal limit on assault weapons. Both were written by Congress. Both can be unwritten by Congress.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate should land harder than this one: guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, and they have been for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In 2023 alone, guns killed 2,566 children and teens, an average of seven young people every day (CDC, 2023). Firearms now kill more children and teens than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, 2025).

Every one of those 2,566 deaths was preventable in the specific, practical ways this brief describes: a sale that could have required a background check, a military-style rifle that could have been off the civilian market, a person in crisis whose firearms could have been temporarily removed by a court. A country that knows the leading cause of death for its children and declines to act on it is not out of ideas. It is out of will.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, federal law has required a background check on gun purchases from licensed dealers. The requirement ends at the shop counter. Federal law does not require a check on most private sales, including many arranged online or at gun shows, which means a person legally barred from having a gun can buy one from an unlicensed seller without ever being screened.

The data show how much of the market slips through. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among private purchases, including person-to-person sales arranged online or at gun shows, half were obtained without a check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Universal background checks close the gap by routing every sale and transfer through the same federal screening system dealers already use. The policy is endorsed across medicine, public health and law enforcement, and it commands overwhelming public support: 81 percent of Americans, including majorities in both parties, back background checks for all gun purchasers (Monmouth University Poll, April 2023). [Hmm — "including majorities in both parties" — verified? Monmouth April 2023: 81% overall; partisan split ~95% Dem / 71% GOP? Not verified. Drop "including majorities in both parties." Actually Monmouth's release likely says "large majorities of Republicans and Democrats," but I can't confirm. Drop it.] 

Replace with: "...and 81 percent of Americans support requiring background checks for all gun purchasers (Monmouth University Poll, April 2023)."

Closing the private-sale gap is the single most basic step available to Congress, and it has been sitting on the table for more than 30 years.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings rose again in 2023. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, roughly one every 13 hours, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692 (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). That is up from 647 in 2022 and second only to the record 689 of 2021.

The weapons involved are no mystery. In Uvalde, Texas, in 2022, a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School with an AR-15-style rifle (ABC News, 2022). In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, a gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds at a bowling alley before attacking a second location, killing 18 people in all (Maine Independent Commission, 2024). From Parkland in 2018 onward, the country's deadliest attacks keep featuring the same signature: semiautomatic rifles built for rapid fire at close range and fed by detachable magazines.

Congress has already tested the alternative. The federal assault weapons ban was in force from 1994 until Congress let it lapse in 2004. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting data from 1981 through 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely to occur in years the ban was in force, a statistically significant difference after controlling for the underlying trend, amounting to nine fewer mass-shooting deaths for every 10,000 firearm homicides (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). The same study found that assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 mass-shooting fatalities documented in its dataset, about 86 percent.

Banning assault weapons is majority opinion, not radical politics. Sixty-four percent of Americans favor a ban, and 66 percent favor prohibiting the high-capacity magazines that make these rifles so lethal in close quarters (Pew Research Center, June 2023).

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that federal law has left open for more than three decades. The policy is backed by 81 percent of Americans (Monmouth University Poll, April 2023).

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban that lapsed in 2004 and update its definitions to cover the rifles and detachable magazines on the market today. 3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Sustain and expand the $25 million annual research investment Congress first provided in fiscal 2020, after more than two decades without dedicated federal research funding (U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee, December 2019). 4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Offer grants to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection orders, which let courts temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be dangerous to themselves or others. Seventy-seven percent of Americans support these laws, including roughly 70 percent of gun owners (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, January 2025), and Connecticut's version is estimated to have averted about one suicide for every 10 gun removals (Swanson et al., 2017).

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026**

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Guns killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, an average of one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year (CDC, 2023).
- The federal background-check requirement stops at the dealer's door. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases involved no check at all (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- Mass shootings rose again in 2023, to 656 incidents that killed 712 people (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). Peer-reviewed research finds mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban (DiMaggio et al., 2019). Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023 (CDC, 2023). That averages out to one death every 11 minutes: 128 people a day, every day, for the entire year. Each of those deaths left an empty chair somewhere, at a kitchen table, in a classroom, on a shift that never ended.

A toll like that is not weather, and it is not geography. It is the accumulation of choices made by the one institution with the power to change them. For more than 30 years Congress has declined to close the two gaps that most define American gun violence: a background-check law that reaches only part of the gun market, and the absence, since 2004, of any federal limit on assault weapons. Year after year, the cost of that refusal is counted in cemeteries, hospital wards and classrooms that will never be full again.

This brief is about both gaps, and about what the evidence says Congress should do about them. The numbers that follow are not abstractions. They are the price of the loopholes, and every one of them is a policy choice the current Congress can reverse.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate should land harder than this one: guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, and they have been for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In 2023 alone, guns killed 2,566 children and teens, an average of seven young people every day (CDC, 2023). Firearms now kill more children and teens than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, 2025).

Every one of those deaths was preventable in the specific ways this brief describes: a sale that could have gone through a background check, a military-style rifle that could have been off the civilian market, a person in crisis whose firearms a court could have temporarily removed. A country that knows the leading cause of death for its children and still declines to act on it is not out of ideas. It is out of will.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, federal law has required a background check on gun purchases from licensed dealers. The requirement ends at the shop counter. Federal law requires no check on most private sales, including many arranged online or at gun shows, which means a person legally barred from having a gun can buy one from an unlicensed seller without ever being screened.

The data show how much of the market slips through. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among private purchases, including person-to-person sales arranged in person, online or at gun shows, half were obtained without a check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Universal background checks close the gap by routing every sale and transfer through the same federal screening system licensed dealers already use. Nothing about it is experimental: the check takes minutes, it is endorsed across medicine, public health and law enforcement, and 86 percent of American adults support requiring background checks on all gun sales and transfers (McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023).

Closing the private-sale gap is the most basic step available to Congress, and it has been sitting on the table for more than 30 years. A loophole that lets half of private gun purchases proceed with no background check is not a detail of the law. It is the law failing at the moment it matters most.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings rose again in 2023. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, roughly one every 13 hours, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692 (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). That is up from 647 in 2022 and second only to the record 689 of 2021.

The weapons involved are no mystery. In Uvalde, Texas, in 2022, a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School with an AR-15-style rifle (ABC News). In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, a gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds at a bowling alley before attacking a second location, killing 18 people in all (Maine Independent Commission, 2024). From Parkland in 2018 onward, the country's deadliest attacks keep featuring the same signature: semiautomatic rifles built for rapid fire at close range, fed by detachable high-capacity magazines.

Congress has already tested the alternative. The federal assault weapons ban was in force from 1994 until Congress allowed it to lapse in 2004. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting data from 1981 through 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely to occur in years the ban was in force, a statistically significant difference after controlling for the underlying trend, equal to nine fewer mass-shooting deaths for every 10,000 firearm homicides (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). The same study found that assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 mass-shooting fatalities documented in its dataset, about 86 percent.

Banning assault weapons is majority opinion, not radical politics. Sixty-four percent of Americans favor a ban, and 66 percent favor prohibiting the high-capacity magazines that make these rifles so lethal in close quarters (Pew Research Center, June 2023).

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that federal law has left open for more than three decades. The policy is backed by 86 percent of American adults (McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023).

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban that lapsed in 2004 and update its definitions to cover the rifles and detachable high-capacity magazines on the market today. A 64 percent majority of Americans supports a ban (Pew Research Center, June 2023), and the evidence indicates it worked: mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely in the ban years (DiMaggio et al., 2019).

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Sustain and expand the dedicated federal research funding Congress began in fiscal 2020, when it provided $25 million for the CDC and NIH after more than two decades without any (U.S. Senate Committee on Appropriations, December 2019). The country cannot prevent what it declines to measure.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Offer grants to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others. Seventy-seven percent of Americans support these laws, including about 70 percent of gun owners (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, January 2025), and Connecticut's version is estimated to have averted roughly one suicide for every 10 gun removals (Swanson et al., 2017).

## Closing the gaps

The gaps in federal gun law were not discovered in nature. Congress wrote the private-sale gap into the Brady Act in 1993 and allowed the assault weapons ban to lapse in 2004. What Congress wrote, Congress can close. The evidence is in, the public is behind it, and the deaths continue at a rate of one every 11 minutes. The only question left is how many more empty chairs the country will count while Congress decides.

---

**About the author.** Dr. Jamal Whitfield is Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at the Northgate Progress Institute, where he leads the Safer Communities series.

*All statistics in this brief are sourced and documented in the accompanying data appendix (Safer Communities Brief No. 9, Data Appendix).*

*Production draft for editorial review under NPI-PUB-2026-0457. Not for release until approved by the Director of Publications.*

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Data appendix

**Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban**

Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026 | Prepared for editorial review under NPI-PUB-2026-0457

## How to read this appendix

One table per figure used in the brief. Source lines follow the house format: agency/author, title, date, URL. Population and methodology notes live in this appendix, not in body copy, the fact sheet or the stat cards (style sheet B1). Derived figures show their derivation. For any chart built from these tables: NPI teal #0F6E6E for the primary series, NPI coral #E4572E for emphasis, y-axis starting at zero (B7).

## Table 1. National gun deaths, 2023 (headline toll)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Total gun deaths, 2023 | 46,728 |
| Average interval between deaths | about 11 minutes |
| Average deaths per day | about 128 |

Notes:
- Underlying data: CDC WONDER final mortality data, 2023.
- Breakdown by intent, 2023 (house style B2 keeps intent breakdowns in the appendix): 27,300 firearm suicides (58 percent of the total) and 17,927 firearm homicides. Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.
- Johns Hopkins describes 2023 as the third-highest annual total ever recorded.
- Derivations: 46,728 deaths across 525,600 minutes is one death every 11.2 minutes ("every 11 minutes," per Johns Hopkins); across 365 days, about 128 deaths per day.

Source: Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions and Johns Hopkins Center for Suicide Prevention, Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic, June 26, 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf

## Table 2. Children and teens (figure: firearms as the leading cause of death)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Gun deaths among children and teens, 2023 | 2,566 |
| Consecutive years as the leading cause of death | 4 (2020 through 2023) |
| Average deaths per day | about 7 |

Notes:
- Age range: 1 through 17 (house style B3 places the age range in the appendix).
- Death rate: 3.7 per 100,000 (2023).
- Firearms kill more children and teens than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins, from CDC WONDER).
- Breakdown by intent, ages 1 through 17, 2023: homicide 63 percent, suicide 29 percent, unintentional 5 percent, undetermined or other 3 percent (Johns Hopkins, from CDC WONDER).
- Derivation: 2,566 deaths across 365 days is about 7 per day.
- Pooled rate for ages 1 through 19, 2021 through 2023: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, from CDC WONDER). Not used in copy.

Source: Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic, June 26, 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf; annual data page, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/annual-gun-violence-data-2023

## Table 3. Background checks (figure: acquisitions made without a check)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Owners who acquired their most recent firearm within the previous two years without a background check | 22 percent (95% confidence interval, 16 to 27 percent) |
| Private purchases obtained without a background check | 50 percent |

Notes:
- "Private" means purchases other than from a store or pawnshop, including sales between individuals in person, online and at gun shows.
- Survey parameters (B1): probability-based national online survey of 1,613 adult gun owners, fielded in 2015.
- The 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook and Ludwig) estimated that about 40 percent of recently acquired guns were obtained without going through a licensed dealer, but that estimate included gifts and inheritances and did not ask directly about background checks. The 2017 Annals survey is the house-standard estimate (B4).
- Federal law has required background checks on sales by licensed dealers since the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act of 1993 (Public Law 103-159), effective February 1994.

Source: Matthew Miller, Lisa Hepburn and Deborah Azrael, Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Annals of Internal Medicine, February 21, 2017, https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M16-1590

## Table 4. Mass shootings, 2023 (figure: Gun Violence Archive mass shooting count)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass shootings, 2023 | 656 |
| People killed | 712 |
| People injured | 2,692 |
| Frequency | about one every 13 hours |
| Comparison years | 647 in 2022; record 689 in 2021 |

Notes:
- Gun Violence Archive definition (B5): a mass shooting is an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter.
- Counts are incident-based, compiled from media and police reporting and revised over time; figures here are as compiled in January 2024.
- Derivation: 656 mass shootings across 8,760 hours is about one every 13 hours.

Sources: Gun Violence Archive, Mass Shootings in 2023, https://www.gunviolencearchive.org/reports/mass-shooting?year=2023; Axios, Mass shootings increased in 2023. But gun deaths went down, January 9, 2024, https://www.axios.com/2024/01/09/mass-shooting-gun-violence-us-2023

## Table 5. The 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban (figure: ban years compared with non-ban years)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Federal ban in force | 1994 through September 13, 2004 |
| Mass-shooting fatalities, ban years versus other years | 70 percent less likely during the ban (relative rate 0.30; 95% confidence interval, 0.22 to 0.39) |
| Mass-shooting deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides | 9 fewer during the ban years |
| Assault rifles' share of documented mass-shooting fatalities | 430 of 501 fatalities (85.8 percent), across 44 incidents |

Notes:
- Study period: 1981 through 2017, open-source mass shooting datasets; the ban-period effect is estimated controlling for yearly trend.
- The ban, title XI of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994 (Public Law 103-322), covered semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices and carried a 10-year sunset. "Assault weapons" in this brief refers to that statutory category, as updated by Congress.

Sources: DiMaggio, Avraham, Berry, et al., Changes in US mass shooting deaths associated with the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban: Analysis of open-source data, Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019, https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0000000000002060; Congressional Research Service, Semiautomatic Assault Weapons Ban, RL32585, December 16, 2004, https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/20041216_RL32585_7078b6a30befc824f752b3b3666ec2e5f038a961.pdf

## Table 6. Federal gun violence research funding (figure: fiscal 2020 research appropriation)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Dedicated federal gun violence research funding, fiscal 2020 | $25 million (CDC and NIH) |
| Prior dedicated federal research funding | none for more than two decades |

Notes: The funding was included in the fiscal 2020 consolidated appropriations agreement and directed to the CDC and NIH for research on firearm injury and mortality prevention.

Source: U.S. Senate Committee on Appropriations, FY2020 Investing in America (summary of the fiscal year 2020 appropriations agreement), December 2019, https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/FY%202020%20Investing%20in%20America.pdf

## Table 7. Extreme-risk law evidence (figure: Connecticut averted-suicide estimate)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Gun removal cases under Connecticut's 1999 risk-warrant law | 762 |
| Estimated averted gun suicides | about 71 |
| Removals per averted suicide | about 10 to 11 |

Notes: Counterfactual analysis based on case fatality rates for the suicide methods people subjected to removal orders would likely have used; removal cases from the law's 1999 enactment through 2013.

Source: Jeffrey W. Swanson, et al., Implementation and Effectiveness of Connecticut's Risk-Based Gun Removal Law: Does It Prevent Suicides?, Law and Contemporary Problems, 2017, https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4830&context=lcp

## Table 8. Public support (polling figures used in the brief)

| Policy | Support | Poll |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Background checks on all gun sales and transfers | 86 percent | McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023 |
| Ban on assault weapons | 64 percent | Pew Research Center, June 2023 |
| Ban on high-capacity magazines (more than 10 rounds) | 66 percent | Pew Research Center, June 2023 |
| Extreme-risk protection orders | 77 percent (about 70 percent of gun owners) | Johns Hopkins National Survey of Gun Policy, January 2025 |

Notes:
- Pew question wording: "banning assault-style weapons" and "banning high-capacity ammunition magazines that hold more than 10 rounds"; the brief uses the house term "assault weapons" (A2).
- Johns Hopkins survey parameters (B1): 2,977 respondents, including 1,001 gun owners, fielded January 6 through 24, 2025.
- The McCourtney Poll measured support for Congress mandating background checks for all firearm sales and transfers, May 12 through 18, 2023.

Sources: APM Research Lab, Americans' views on gun policy, background checks, assault weapons bans, Second Amendment (McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll), May 2023, https://www.apmresearchlab.org/motn/americans-views-on-gun-policy-background-checks-assault-weapons-bans-second-amendment; Pew Research Center, Americans' views of specific gun policy proposals, June 28, 2023, https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/06/28/americans-views-of-specific-gun-policy-proposals/; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, National Survey of Gun Policy, January 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/national-survey-of-gun-policy

## Table 9. Named incidents referenced in the brief

| Incident | Date | Killed | Injured | Weapon |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, Parkland, Florida | February 14, 2018 | 17 | 17 | Smith & Wesson M&P15 (AR-15-style) |
| Robb Elementary School, Uvalde, Texas | May 24, 2022 | 21 (19 children and two teachers) | 17 | Daniel Defense DDM4 V7 (AR-15-style) |
| Lewiston, Maine (two locations) | October 25, 2023 | 18 | 13 by gunfire | Ruger SFAR .308 (AR-10-style) |

Notes: Killed and injured counts exclude the shooters. At the first Lewiston location, a bowling alley, the gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds; Lewiston was the deadliest U.S. mass shooting of 2023. No individual victims are named in the brief, per the author's outline.

Sources: Gun Violence Archive, school shootings incident database, https://www.gunviolencearchive.org/school-shootings; ABC News, Maine massacre among worst mass shootings in modern U.S. history, October 2023, https://abcnews.com/US/texas-school-shooting-7th-deadliest-mass-shooting-recent/story?id=84966004; Violence Policy Center, large-capacity ammunition magazine shooting list, https://vpc.org/fact_sht/VPCshootinglist.pdf; Independent Commission to Investigate the Facts of the Tragedy in Lewiston, Final Report, 2024, https://www.maine.gov/icl/sites/maine.gov.icl/files/2024-08/Final%20Report%20Of%20The%20Independent%20Commission%20To%20Investigate%20The%20Facts%20Of%20The%20Tragedy%20In%20Lewiston.pdf

---

# NPI brief urges Congress to pass universal background checks and reinstate the assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 documents the toll behind the two biggest gaps in federal gun law

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Northgate Progress Institute today released Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, an average of one death every 11 minutes, and guns remain the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year (CDC data). Yet 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases involved no check (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017). The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, up from 647 in 2022, and peer-reviewed research finds mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban (Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019).

"The gaps in our gun laws were written by Congress, and only Congress can close them," Whitfield said. "One death every 11 minutes is not a fact of nature. It is a policy choice, and Congress makes it again every day it declines to act. Universal background checks and a renewed assault weapons ban have the evidence behind them and the country behind them. What is missing is the will."

The brief recommends that Congress:

- Pass universal background checks.
- Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.
- Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.
- Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026**

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Guns killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, an average of one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year (CDC, 2023).
- The federal background-check requirement stops at the dealer's door. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of all private purchases involved no check at all (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- Mass shootings rose again in 2023, to 656 incidents that killed 712 people (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). Peer-reviewed research finds mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely during the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban (DiMaggio et al., 2019). Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023 (CDC, 2023). That averages out to one death every 11 minutes: 128 people a day, every day, for the entire year. Each of those deaths left an empty chair somewhere, at a kitchen table, in a classroom, on a shift that never ended.

A toll like that is not weather, and it is not geography. It is the accumulation of choices made by the one institution with the power to change them. For more than 30 years Congress has declined to close the two gaps that most define American gun violence: a background-check law that reaches only part of the gun market, and the absence, since 2004, of any federal limit on assault weapons. Year after year, the cost of that refusal is counted in cemeteries, hospital wards and classrooms that will never be full again.

This brief is about both gaps, and about what the evidence says Congress should do about them. The numbers that follow are not abstractions. They are the price of the loopholes, and every one of them is a policy choice the current Congress can reverse.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate should land harder than this one: guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens, and they have been for four consecutive years (CDC, 2023). In 2023 alone, guns killed 2,566 children and teens, an average of seven young people every day (CDC, 2023). Firearms now kill more children and teens than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, 2025).

Every one of those deaths was preventable in the specific ways this brief describes: a sale that could have gone through a background check, a military-style rifle that could have been off the civilian market, a person in crisis whose firearms a court could have temporarily removed. A country that knows the leading cause of death for its children and still declines to act on it is not out of ideas. It is out of will.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect in 1994, federal law has required a background check on gun purchases from licensed dealers. The requirement ends at the shop counter. Federal law requires no check on most private sales, including many arranged online or at gun shows, which means a person legally barred from having a gun can buy one from an unlicensed seller without ever being screened.

The data show how much of the market slips through. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among private purchases, including person-to-person sales arranged in person, online or at gun shows, half were obtained without a check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).

Universal background checks close the gap by routing every sale and transfer through the same federal screening system licensed dealers already use. Nothing about it is experimental: the check takes minutes, it is endorsed across medicine, public health and law enforcement, and 86 percent of American adults support requiring background checks on all gun sales and transfers (McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023).

Closing the private-sale gap is the most basic step available to Congress, and it has been sitting on the table for more than 30 years. A loophole that lets half of private gun purchases proceed with no background check is not a detail of the law. It is the law failing at the moment it matters most.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings rose again in 2023. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings, roughly one every 13 hours, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692 (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). That is up from 647 in 2022 and second only to the record 689 of 2021.

The weapons involved are no mystery. In Uvalde, Texas, in 2022, a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School with an AR-15-style rifle (ABC News). In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, a gunman fired 18 rounds in 45 seconds at a bowling alley before attacking a second location, killing 18 people in all (Maine Independent Commission, 2024). From Parkland in 2018 onward, the country's deadliest attacks keep featuring the same signature: semiautomatic rifles built for rapid fire at close range, fed by detachable high-capacity magazines.

Congress has already tested the alternative. The federal assault weapons ban was in force from 1994 until Congress allowed it to lapse in 2004. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting data from 1981 through 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely to occur in years the ban was in force, a statistically significant difference after controlling for the underlying trend, equal to nine fewer mass-shooting deaths for every 10,000 firearm homicides (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019). The same study found that assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 mass-shooting fatalities documented in its dataset, about 86 percent.

Banning assault weapons is majority opinion, not radical politics. Sixty-four percent of Americans favor a ban, and 66 percent favor prohibiting the high-capacity magazines that make these rifles so lethal in close quarters (Pew Research Center, June 2023).

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale gap that federal law has left open for more than three decades. The policy is backed by 86 percent of American adults (McCourtney Institute Mood of the Nation Poll, May 2023).

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban that lapsed in 2004 and update its definitions to cover the rifles and detachable high-capacity magazines on the market today. A 64 percent majority of Americans supports a ban (Pew Research Center, June 2023), and the evidence indicates it worked: mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely in the ban years (DiMaggio et al., 2019).

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Sustain and expand the dedicated federal research funding Congress began in fiscal 2020, when it provided $25 million for the CDC and NIH after more than two decades without any (U.S. Senate Committee on Appropriations, December 2019). The country cannot prevent what it declines to measure.

4. **Incentivize state extreme-risk laws.** Offer grants to states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others. Seventy-seven percent of Americans support these laws, including about 70 percent of gun owners (Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, January 2025), and Connecticut's version is estimated to have averted roughly one suicide for every 10 gun removals (Swanson et al., 2017).

## Closing the gaps

The gaps in federal gun law were not discovered in nature. Congress wrote the private-sale gap into the Brady Act in 1993 and allowed the assault weapons ban to lapse in 2004. What Congress wrote, Congress can close. The evidence is in, the public is behind it, and the deaths continue at a rate of one every 11 minutes. The only question left is how many more empty chairs the country will count while Congress decides.

---

**About the author.** Dr. Jamal Whitfield is Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at the Northgate Progress Institute, where he leads the Safer Communities series.

*All statistics in this brief are sourced and documented in the accompanying data appendix (Safer Communities Brief No. 9, Data Appendix).*

*Production draft for editorial review under NPI-PUB-2026-0457. Not for release until approved by the Director of Publications.*
